items.text: Teaching was already going on at Oxford by 1096, while the Aztec capital Tenochtitlán wasn't founded until 1325.
items.note: Oxford has no exact founding date, only evidence of teaching by 1096. Counting the Aztec Empire from its 1428 alliance instead of the city's founding makes the gap even bigger.

sources.title: The University of Oxford Is Older Than the Aztec Empire and Other Facts That Will Change Your Perspective on History

items.text: The Aztec Empire took shape in 1428 and fell to Spanish forces and their Indigenous allies in 1521, less than a century later. The White House has now stood longer than that.
items.note: The White House cornerstone was laid in 1792, about 234 years ago. Even counting from Tenochtitlán's founding in 1325, the city lasted only about 196 years until 1521.

sources.title: The University of Oxford Is Older Than the Aztec Empire and Other Facts That Will Change Your Perspective on History

items.text: In 1167, England's King Henry II banned English students from attending the University of Paris during a feud with Archbishop Thomas Becket. That sent a wave of students to Oxford.
items.note: The Smithsonian says Oxford 'welcomed an influx' of students after the ban. It is one reason Oxford grew quickly, not the only one.

sources.title: The University of Oxford Is Older Than the Aztec Empire and Other Facts That Will Change Your Perspective on History

items.text: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of August 27, 1896 lasted no longer than 40 minutes, making it the shortest war in recorded history.
items.note: Sources give slightly different lengths, from about 38 to 45 minutes, depending on when the clock starts and stops.

items.text: Woolly mammoths outlived the Great Pyramid. A small group survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago, so they were contemporaries of the Egyptian pyramids.
items.note: Most mammoths died out around 10,000 years ago. The Great Pyramid dates to about 2560 BCE, roughly 4,500 years ago, so the overlap is a few centuries at most for the pyramid builders.

sources.title: Wrangel Island: Land of Mammoths, Explorers, and Polar Bears

items.text: In 1932 Australia ran a military operation to stop emus from wrecking crops in Western Australia, and it was unsuccessful. Politicians joked that if anyone deserved medals, it was the emus.
items.note: It is called the 'Emu War', but it was a culling operation that soldiers with machine guns carried out. The 'emu victory' label is a joke from the time.

items.text: Vikings were cutting trees in Newfoundland in exactly 1021. Tree rings show a Viking ax felled trees on the North American continent in 1021 C.E. That was about 471 years before Columbus.
items.note: Scientists matched a spike in carbon-14 in the tree rings, caused by a solar storm in 993 CE, to count forward to the cutting year. This confirms the Norse were there by 1021 and they may have arrived earlier.

sources.title: First Viking settlement in North America dated to exactly 1000 years ago
Evidence for European presence in the Americas in ad 1021
Archaeologists used tree rings and astrophysics to prove Vikings were in Canada in 1021

items.text: The pyramid builders were not slaves. Their tombs near the Giza pyramids held jars that once contained beer and bread meant for the workers' afterlife.
items.note: Egypt's archaeology chief at the time, Zahi Hawass, argued that the builders were paid laborers. The work was still hard and dangerous, and Egypt did have slaves in this period; they just weren't the main workforce here.

sources.title: Egypt displays tombs of pyramid builders
Egypt discovers workers' tombs near pyramids

items.text: The Greek historian Herodotus wrote that 100,000 people built the pyramids, but Egypt's antiquities chief estimated about 10,000 workers over more than 30 years for a single pyramid.
items.note: The 10,000 figure is one expert's estimate, not a settled count. Herodotus visited Egypt around 450 BCE, about 2,000 years after the pyramids were built.
